text: Fabric enforces throttling at the capacity level rather than the tenant level, so a saturated capacity only affects the workspaces assigned to it; other capacities continue operating normally.

Fabric uses two complementary mechanisms — bursting (letting an operation consume more CUs than the SKU provision allows so it completes quickly) and smoothing (spreading that consumed CU cost across future timepoints) — to avoid penalizing users for temporary spikes.

A Fabric timepoint is 30 seconds long. There are 2,880 timepoints in a 24-hour window, and smoothing distributes an operation's CU cost across those future timepoints rather than charging the full amount at submission.

Interactive operations are smoothed over a minimum of 5 minutes and up to 64 minutes depending on their total CU consumption, while background operations are always smoothed over a full 24-hour window because they typically carry much larger CU loads.

Throttling is staged progressively across four thresholds keyed to how much future capacity has been consumed: up to 10 minutes of future usage triggers no throttling (overage protection); between 10 and 60 minutes triggers a 20-second delay on new interactive operations; between 60 minutes and 24 hours causes interactive operations to be rejected outright while background operations may still start; beyond 24 hours all new requests — interactive and background alike — are rejected.

When accumulated future-capacity usage exceeds the 10-minute overage protection window, the excess is recorded as carryforward CUs. Each subsequent timepoint that has idle capacity reduces this carryforward balance through a process called burndown. Throttling enforcement continues until the full carryforward balance reaches zero.
Operations that were already in flight when a capacity enters a throttling state are always allowed to run to completion; only new operation submissions are subject to delay or rejection.
When a capacity rejects requests, users receive HTTP status code CapacityLimitExceeded along with error messages indicating that compute capacity limits have been reached.

Three workload-specific exceptions exist to the standard throttling rules: Fabric Eventstreams reduce allocated CU resources rather than delaying or rejecting new stream operations; Real-Time Intelligence skips the 20-second interactive delay stage and only begins throttling at the 60-minute rejection threshold; and Warehouse operations are classified as background to benefit from 24-hour smoothing, though a background operation triggered by an interactive chain can be promoted to interactive throttling rules.

Fabric provides compound throttling protection so that a single end-user request that fans out into a chain of dependent operations (for example a report visual querying a semantic model that reads from OneLake) is throttled at most once per capacity in the chain, preventing the same request from being penalised multiple times.

The throttling system classifies operations at submission time before execution begins, so classification can change once runtime information becomes available. In ambiguous cases the system defaults to the background classification, which favours the user by applying the more lenient 24-hour smoothing window.
Bursting and smoothing do not apply when a capacity admin has enabled Autoscale Billing for Spark; in that configuration Spark usage operates in pay-as-you-go mode only.

Each Fabric capacity is a distinct resource pool living inside a Microsoft Entra tenant; the SKU size determines how much compute power the pool provides, and a tenant can hold as many capacities as the organization needs — often aligned to geography or business unit.
